about: Hand-authored reference for Ruby 3.4, covering the built-in methods, keywords and error classes a beginner's program is most likely to use. Written from accurate knowledge of Ruby semantics; not copied verbatim from any external source. Entries cover documented failure modes (puts blank-line myth, elsif vs elif) plus the constructs that appear in almost every beginner Ruby file. Used by server/src/ruby-reference.js; attached to each tutor message about a .rb file.

ArgumentError.text:
ArgumentError

Raised when a method receives the wrong number of arguments, or an argument that is not valid for that method.

  def add(a, b); a + b; end
  add(1)          # ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (given 1, expected 2)
  add(1, 2, 3)    # ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (given 3, expected 2)

Also raised by Integer() and Float() when the string cannot be converted:
  Integer("abc")  # ArgumentError: invalid value for Integer(): "abc"

Contrast: to_i and to_f never raise — they return 0 or 0.0 on bad input instead.

NameError.text:
NameError

Raised when a name (variable, method, or constant) cannot be found.

  puts undefined_var  # NameError: undefined local variable or method 'undefined_var'

In Ruby, elif is not a keyword. Ruby reads `elif x > 3` as a call to a method named elif. If no such method exists, running that line raises NoMethodError (a subclass of NameError) — but only when execution reaches that branch. A file that never enters the branch will not show the error, which is why a run can end cleanly while the bug is still present.

NoMethodError.text:
NoMethodError

Raised when a method is called on an object that does not define it. The message names the method and the class of the receiver.

  nil.length      # NoMethodError: undefined method 'length' for nil
  42.upcase       # NoMethodError: undefined method 'upcase' for an instance of Integer

Most common causes in beginner code:
- A variable is nil because it was never assigned, or a method returned nil.
- gets returns a String (e.g. "42\n"); calling .to_i on it is fine, but calling a String method after .to_i (which returns an Integer) gives NoMethodError.
- A method name is misspelled (Ruby reads it as an undefined method call).
- Using elif instead of elsif: Ruby reads elif as a method name, and calling it raises NoMethodError when that line runs.

TypeError.text:
TypeError

Raised when a value is not of the type the operation requires.

  "hello" + 42      # TypeError: no implicit conversion of Integer into String
  [1, 2] + "x"      # TypeError: no implicit conversion of String into Array

Ruby does not coerce types automatically. Convert explicitly before mixing:
  "hello" + 42.to_s   # => "hello42"
  "3".to_i + 4        # => 7
  "3" + "4"           # => "34"  (string concatenation)

ZeroDivisionError.text:
ZeroDivisionError

Raised when an integer is divided by zero.

  10 / 0     # ZeroDivisionError: divided by 0

Float division by zero does not raise — it returns Infinity:
  10.0 / 0   # => Infinity
  -1.0 / 0   # => -Infinity
  0.0 / 0    # => NaN

chomp.text:
str.chomp → new_str
str.chomp(separator) → new_str

Returns a new string with the trailing record separator removed. The default separator is \n, \r\n, or \r. Returns the original string unchanged if it does not end with a separator. Does not modify the original (use chomp! to modify in place).

  "hello\n".chomp    # => "hello"
  "hello\r\n".chomp  # => "hello"
  "hello".chomp      # => "hello"  (no change)
  "hello\n\n".chomp  # => "hello\n"  (removes only one trailing newline)

The most common use: removing the newline that gets always appends.
  name = gets.chomp   # user types Alice → name is "Alice", not "Alice\n"

class.text:
class ClassName
  def initialize(params)
    @instance_variable = value
  end

  def method_name
    # ...
  end
end

Defines a class. Class names must begin with an uppercase letter (convention: CamelCase). Instance variables begin with @. The initialize method runs automatically when a new instance is created with ClassName.new(arguments).

  class Dog
    def initialize(name)
      @name = name
    end
    def speak
      puts "#{@name} says Woof!"
    end
  end

  dog = Dog.new("Rex")
  dog.speak    # prints: Rex says Woof!

Every class definition ends with end.

def.text:
def method_name(param1, param2, ...)
  # body
end

Defines a method. The last evaluated expression in the body is the return value — an explicit return is optional. Parameters can have defaults: def greet(name = "World").

  def add(a, b)
    a + b          # returned implicitly
  end

  def greet(name = "World")
    "Hello, #{name}!"
  end

  puts add(3, 4)      # => 7
  puts greet          # => Hello, World!
  puts greet("Alice") # => Hello, Alice!

Every def ends with end. Methods defined outside any class become private methods of Object and are callable anywhere.

downcase.text:
str.downcase → new_str

Returns a new string with all letters lowercased. Does not modify the original (use downcase! to modify in place).

  "HELLO".downcase      # => "hello"
  "Hello World".downcase # => "hello world"

See also: upcase (uppercases all letters), capitalize (first letter upper, rest lower).

each.text:
array.each { |element| block } → array
array.each do |element|
  block
end → array

Calls the block once for each element in the array, passing that element as the argument. Returns the original array.

  [1, 2, 3].each { |n| puts n }
  # prints:
  # 1
  # 2
  # 3

  words = ["cat", "dog", "bird"]
  words.each do |word|
    puts word.upcase
  end
  # prints: CAT, DOG, BIRD

Both { } and do...end are valid block syntax. Convention: { } for one-liners, do...end for multi-line blocks.

for.text:
for variable in collection
  # body
end

Iterates over each element in collection, assigning it to variable. Ranges (1..5, 1...5) are common collections.

  for i in 1..5
    puts i
  end
  # prints: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5  (.. includes the endpoint)

  for i in 1...5
    puts i
  end
  # prints: 1, 2, 3, 4  (... excludes the endpoint)

Unlike .each, for does not create a new scope: the loop variable remains accessible after the loop ends. In Ruby idiom, .each is more commonly used than for.

gets.text:
gets(sep=$/) → string or nil

Reads the next line from standard input (what the user typed), including the trailing newline character (\n). Returns nil at end of input.

The returned string always includes the newline:
  name = gets        # user types Alice → name is "Alice\n" (with \n)

Use chomp to remove the trailing newline before using the value:
  name = gets.chomp  # name is "Alice"

To read a number:
  age = gets.chomp.to_i    # string → remove newline → integer
  price = gets.chomp.to_f  # string → remove newline → float

If gets is not followed by chomp, the trailing \n will be part of string operations and comparisons, which is almost always wrong.

if.text:
if condition
  # body
elsif another_condition
  # body
else
  # body
end

Executes the matching body when its condition is truthy. In Ruby, only false and nil are falsy — everything else (including 0, "", and []) is truthy.

The keyword is elsif — not elif (Python) and not else if (JavaScript/C). A bare elif is not a Ruby keyword: Ruby reads `elif x > 3` as a call to a method named elif, which raises NoMethodError when that line runs. The error appears only if execution reaches that branch, so a program that never enters the elsif can run without any visible error.

  if score >= 90
    puts "A"
  elsif score >= 80
    puts "B"
  else
    puts "C"
  end

Every if block ends with end. Inline (modifier) form: puts "Passing" if score >= 60

length.text:
str.length → integer
str.size → integer

Returns the number of characters in str. length and size are aliases; both work identically.

  "hello".length   # => 5
  "".length        # => 0
  "café".length    # => 4  (characters, not bytes)

For arrays, .length / .size returns the number of elements:
  [1, 2, 3].length # => 3

nil.text:
nil

The sole instance of NilClass, representing the absence of a value. In Ruby, only nil and false are falsy; everything else — including 0, 0.0, and "" — is truthy.

  nil.nil?    # => true
  nil.to_i    # => 0
  nil.to_f    # => 0.0
  nil.to_s    # => ""  (empty string)
  nil.to_a    # => []  (empty array)
  nil.inspect # => "nil"

Calling any other method on nil raises NoMethodError:
  nil.length  # NoMethodError: undefined method 'length' for nil

Common causes of unexpected nil: a variable never assigned; a method that returns nil when it finds nothing (e.g. Array#find with no match); gets at end of input.

p.text:
p(obj) → obj
p(obj1, obj2, ...) → [obj1, obj2, ...]
p() → nil

Writes obj.inspect to stdout, followed by a newline, for each argument. Returns the argument (or an array of arguments if more than one).

Unlike puts, p shows the internal representation of the value:
  p "hello"    # prints: "hello"   (with quotes)
  puts "hello" # prints: hello     (no quotes)
  p nil        # prints: nil
  puts nil     # prints: (blank line)
  p 42         # prints: 42
  p [1,2,3]    # prints: [1, 2, 3]

Mainly used for debugging — it shows exactly what a value is, including whether a string has a trailing newline.

pop.text:
array.pop → obj or nil
array.pop(n) → new_array

Removes and returns the last element of the array. Returns nil if the array is empty (does not raise an error). With an integer argument n, removes and returns the last n elements as a new array.

  arr = [1, 2, 3]
  arr.pop     # => 3;  arr is now [1, 2]
  arr.pop     # => 2;  arr is now [1]
  [].pop      # => nil

print.text:
print(obj, ...) → nil

Writes each argument to stdout, converting to a string with to_s. Unlike puts, print adds no newline after any argument. The cursor stays on the same line after print finishes.

  print "hello"
  print " world"
  # On screen: hello world  (no newline; cursor remains on that line)

  print "hello\n"  # adds a newline explicitly

To move to the next line, either add \n inside the string or use puts instead.

Contrast:
- puts adds a newline after each argument
- print adds nothing
- p calls .inspect and adds a newline

push.text:
array.push(obj, ...) → array
array << obj → array

Appends one or more objects to the end of the array. Returns the array itself (so calls can be chained). << is the append operator and is the more common idiom.

  arr = [1, 2, 3]
  arr.push(4)      # arr => [1, 2, 3, 4]
  arr << 5         # arr => [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  arr << 6 << 7    # arr => [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]

puts.text:
puts(obj, ...) → nil

Writes each argument to stdout, converting to a string with to_s, and appends exactly one newline after each. Called with no arguments, writes a single newline (producing a blank line on screen). If a string argument already ends with a newline, no extra newline is added.

Two consecutive puts calls produce two consecutive lines with no blank line between them:
  puts "hello"
  puts "world"
  # On screen:
  # hello
  # world
  # (no blank line between them)

To print a blank line, call puts with no argument:
  puts "hello"
  puts          # blank line
  puts "world"
  # On screen:
  # hello
  #             (blank line)
  # world

Contrast:
- print adds no newline at all
- p calls .inspect (shows string quotes) and adds a newline
- puts nil prints a blank line (same as puts with no argument)

times.text:
int.times { |i| block } → int
int.times → enumerator

Executes the block int times, passing the current iteration count as the block argument. The count starts at 0 and ends at int-1.

  5.times { |i| puts i }
  # prints: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

  3.times { puts "hello" }
  # prints: hello (three times)

  5.times do |i|
    puts "Iteration #{i}"
  end
  # prints: Iteration 0, Iteration 1, ..., Iteration 4

to_f.text:
str.to_f → float

Returns the result of interpreting the leading characters of str as a floating-point number. Returns 0.0 if str cannot be converted. Never raises.

  "3.14".to_f     # => 3.14
  "42".to_f       # => 42.0
  "  3.14  ".to_f # => 3.14  (leading whitespace ignored)
  "3.14abc".to_f  # => 3.14  (stops at 'a')
  "abc".to_f      # => 0.0

To read a float from the user: gets.chomp.to_f

to_i.text:
str.to_i(base=10) → integer

Returns the result of interpreting the leading characters of str as an integer. Stops at the first character that is not a valid digit in the given base. Returns 0 if str cannot be converted. Never raises.

  "42".to_i        # => 42
  "  42  ".to_i    # => 42  (leading whitespace ignored)
  "3.14".to_i      # => 3   (stops at the decimal point)
  "123abc".to_i    # => 123 (stops at 'a')
  "abc".to_i       # => 0

To read an integer from the user: gets.chomp.to_i

Note: to_i never raises. Use Integer(str) if you want an error on invalid input.

to_s.text:
integer.to_s(base=10) → string
float.to_s → string

Returns a string representation of the number.

  42.to_s      # => "42"
  3.14.to_s    # => "3.14"
  255.to_s(16) # => "ff"  (hexadecimal)
  8.to_s(2)    # => "1000" (binary)

Ruby does not automatically convert numbers to strings for concatenation. Use to_s or string interpolation:
  "Age: " + age.to_s      # explicit conversion
  "Age: #{age}"           # string interpolation (preferred idiom)

unless.text:
unless condition
  # body
else
  # body
end

Executes the body when condition is falsy (false or nil). Equivalent to if !condition. There is no elsunless keyword; use if/elsif/else for multiple branches.

  unless score >= 60
    puts "Failing"
  end

  # One-line modifier form:
  puts "Failing" unless score >= 60

until.text:
until condition
  # body
end

Repeats the body as long as condition is falsy. Equivalent to while !condition. The condition is checked before each iteration.

  i = 0
  until i >= 5
    puts i
    i += 1
  end
  # prints: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

upcase.text:
str.upcase → new_str

Returns a new string with all letters uppercased. Does not modify the original string (use upcase! to modify in place).

  "hello".upcase       # => "HELLO"
  "Hello World".upcase # => "HELLO WORLD"

See also: downcase (all lowercase), capitalize (first letter upper, rest lower), swapcase.

while.text:
while condition
  # body
end

Repeats the body as long as condition is truthy. The condition is checked before each iteration; if it is false or nil on the first check, the body never runs.

  i = 0
  while i < 5
    puts i
    i += 1
  end
  # prints: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

Every while block ends with end. Ruby has no do...while loop; use loop { break if condition } instead.
